prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: I am not sure / that the red car / in the parking slot / is yours.
explanation: After 'not sure', doubt is expressed with 'whether/if', not 'that'; so it should read 'I am not sure whether the red car ... is yours'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: The manager said, "Could you please / confirm to me that you / have received all the items / that you had ordered?"
explanation: The past perfect 'had ordered' has no past reference point since the main verb is the present perfect 'have received'; it should be 'that you have ordered' (or simply 'ordered').

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: He was doubtful that (a) / the man who had been run over (b) / by some vehicles had lain there for more than a day (c) / no error (d)
options: the man who had been run over
by some vehicles had lain there for more than a day
explanation: 'Doubtful' in an affirmative sentence is followed by 'whether' (or 'if'), not 'that': 'He was doubtful whether the man ...'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: I don't know if any of the members (a) / of the party is conspiring (b) / against the President or not. (c) / no error (d)
options: I don't know if any of the members
explanation: When the alternative 'or not' is expressed, the correct conjunction is 'whether', not 'if': 'I don't know whether any of the members ... or not'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: He asked me that I was (a) / preparing for the Civil service (b) / Examinations. (c) / no error (d)
options: He asked me that I was
explanation: An indirect question after 'asked' takes 'whether/if', not 'that': 'He asked me whether I was preparing ...'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: The patient would not have died (a) / when the doctor had (b) / come on time. (c) / no error (d)
options: The patient would not have died
explanation: A third-conditional sentence needs the conditional 'if', not the time word 'when': 'The patient would not have died if the doctor had come on time'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: I cannot confirm (a) / you if he had paid (b) / the bill or returned the goods. (c) / no error (d)
options: the bill or returned the goods.
explanation: 'Confirm' takes the person with the preposition 'to', and a doubtful alternative needs 'whether': 'I cannot confirm to you whether he had paid ...'.

prompt: Identify the part with the grammatical error (or 'No error').
sentence: The project coordinator was highly confused (A) / whether to allocate the additional funds to marketing (B) / or to spend it entirely on technical research. (C) / No Error (D)
options: The project coordinator was highly confused
whether to allocate the additional funds to marketing
or to spend it entirely on technical research.
explanation: The pronoun 'it' does not agree with the plural antecedent 'the additional funds'; it should be 'or to spend them entirely on technical research'.

prompt: Find the part of the sentence that contains an error:
sentence: The manager could not decide whether to approve the merger (1)/ or if the announcement were merely a diversion (2)/ intended to calm investors (3)/ after the recent financial losses. (4)/
explanation: 'Whether' must be balanced by 'or whether' (or a bare 'or'), not 'or if'; also the indicative 'was' is required rather than 'were'.

sentence: Parts of the following sentence are given as options. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. I shall buy this book if you like it or not.
explanation: With the '...or not' construction, 'whether' must be used instead of 'if': 'whether you like it or not'.

prompt: Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose ‘No error’.
sentence: It turns out that my father isn’t alone.
explanation: The sentence is grammatically correct: 'It turns out that' introduces a noun clause and 'alone' is used correctly as a predicative adjective.

prompt: Direction: Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
sentence: It seems (A)/the I am the most(B)/ beautiful plant(C)/ in this forest(D).
explanation: The conjunction 'that' is needed after 'It seems', not the article 'the'; correct form is 'It seems that I am the most beautiful plant'.

explanation: 'Deny' reports a statement, not a doubt, so it takes the conjunction 'that', never 'if'.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution required’.
sentence: I cannot tell you now whether I will be able to come or not.
explanation: 'Whether ... or not' is the correct pair for expressing an unresolved alternative; 'unless', 'because' and 'in case' do not fit the sense of doubt.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution’.
sentence: She asked from me that I had seen the movie or not.
explanation: 'Ask' takes a direct object without 'from', and an indirect question needs 'whether' rather than 'that ... or not'; the past perfect 'had seen' matches the past reporting verb.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No improvement required’.
sentence: Newton, after seeing the apple falling from a tree, began to wonder whether if it moved towards the earth and not upwards towards the sky.
explanation: 'Whether if' is a double conjunction; the sense is a reason, so 'began to wonder why' is correct.

prompt: Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
sentence: Rishi asked Karan will he get a new football for him?

if he would get a new football for him.
if would he get a new football for him?
if he will get a new football for him?
explanation: Reported yes/no questions use 'if' with statement word order and back-shifted tense, ending with a full stop.
